questions.stem: A freely suspended magnetic needle always comes to rest pointing approximately:
questions.explanation: A suspended magnet aligns with Earth's magnetic field, which runs roughly north-south. The magnet's 'N-seeking' pole points to the geographic North (near which lies Earth's magnetic South Pole — because opposite poles attract). The small angular difference between geographic and magnetic north is called 'magnetic declination'. Mariner's compasses exploit this alignment.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The magnetic north pole of the Earth is located near the:
questions.explanation: Counter-intuitive but true — Earth's north-seeking compass pole is attracted to the Arctic, so the magnetic S-pole of Earth is near the geographic North Pole, and Earth's magnetic N-pole is near the geographic South Pole. Unlike poles attract. The magnetic poles wander and have flipped many times in geological history (records preserved in cooled lava).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A temporary magnet — produced only when electric current flows through a coil around an iron core — is called an:
questions.explanation: An electromagnet — coil + soft iron core — behaves as a strong magnet only while current flows, and loses magnetism when switched off. Used in electric bells, motors, MRI machines, magnetic cranes lifting scrap. Permanent magnets (alloys like neodymium-iron-boron) retain magnetism indefinitely. Diamagnets are weakly repelled by external fields (copper, bismuth). Paramagnets weakly align with them (aluminium).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Which of the following materials is ferromagnetic (strongly magnetic)?
questions.explanation: Iron — and its siblings nickel and cobalt, plus some rare earths (gadolinium) — are ferromagnetic; they can be strongly magnetised. Copper is diamagnetic (weakly repelled). Aluminium is paramagnetic (weakly attracted). Wood is essentially non-magnetic. The mnemonic 'iron, nickel, cobalt + few rare earths' covers the room-temperature ferromagnets encountered in everyday physics.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The SI unit of magnetic flux density (also called the strength of the magnetic field) is the:
questions.explanation: Tesla (T) is the SI unit of magnetic flux density — named after Nikola Tesla. Earth's field ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁵ T; a fridge magnet ≈ 10⁻² T; MRI machines ≈ 1-3 T. Weber (Wb) is the unit of total magnetic flux (through a surface). Henry (H) is the unit of inductance. Ampere is the unit of electric current.

questions.stem: Hans Christian Oersted's famous 1820 experiment showed that:

options.option_text: A magnet exerts a force on another magnet
A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it
Light has the same speed in all media
Objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum

questions.explanation: Oersted (1820) found that a compass needle near a current-carrying wire deflects — showing that electricity and magnetism are linked. This single observation founded the subject of electromagnetism. It was followed in 1831 by Faraday's discovery that a changing magnetic field can induce an electric current (electromagnetic induction) — the basis for generators and transformers.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The rule used to find the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying straight conductor is:
questions.explanation: Right-hand thumb rule (sometimes called Maxwell's / Ampere's rule) — hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb pointing along the direction of the current; the curl of the fingers gives the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire. Fleming's left-hand rule — force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (motor rule). Fleming's right-hand rule — direction of induced current in a conductor moving in a field (generator rule). Lenz's law fixes the direction of induced current (opposes the change causing it).
